summary: Outlines how the IETF appoints its representatives to the Community Coordination Group, which advises the IETF Trust on IANA trademarks and domain names.

plainLanguage.summary: The rules for how the IETF picks people for a committee that looks after some important names.

questions: who can be a ccg representative
what is the community coordination group
subtitle: How the IAB picks, removes and reports on the IETF's three seats on the group that advises on IANA trademarks and domain names.

tldr.problem: After the IANA Stewardship Transition, the IETF needed a defined way to choose its three representatives on the Community Coordination Group (CCG), which advises the IETF Trust on the IANA trademarks and domain names.
tldr.mechanism: The IAB makes a public call for nominations, publishes the list of candidates, weighs community feedback and conflicts, and votes. It also handles removal requests, confirms the co-chair and receives reports.
tldr.outcome: The document is an Informational IAB statement of process, not a protocol, and it says it has no implications for network security.

today: RFC 8090 is an Informational RFC from the IAB, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It records the IETF's appointment procedures as published in February 2017.

sections.title: Why the CCG Exists
sections.content:
The IANA IPR Community Agreement was one of the documents that formed part of the IANA Stewardship Transition. It calls for a Community Coordination Group (CCG) to give guidance and advice to the IETF Trust about the IANA Intellectual Property, meaning the IANA trademarks and the IANA domain names.

The CCG has nine individuals, called CCG Representatives. The three operational communities (Names, Numbers and Protocol Parameters) each appoint three. Each community decides for itself how to select, appoint and remove its own representatives. This RFC covers only the IETF side, the Protocol Parameters Community.
sections.plainLanguage: Three groups each send three people to one committee. This RFC says how one of the groups, the IETF, chooses its three.

sections.title: Desirable Qualifications
sections.content:
Candidates should have a demonstrable involvement in the IETF and a solid understanding of how the IETF uses protocol parameter registries. They should know how the IETF community depends on the IANA trademarks and domain names.

Candidates are also expected to show technical competence in managing IANA protocol parameter registries, to understand how the Names Community and the Numbers Community use IANA registries, and to be able to call on others in the IETF community to get the best advice to the IETF Trust.
sections.plainLanguage: The people picked should know the IETF well and understand the lists that IANA keeps, like a good librarian who also knows who to ask for help.

sections.title: Selection Procedures
sections.content:
The three representatives serve at the pleasure of the IAB. Each is expected to serve at least a year, and appointments ought to be staggered so that all three are not replaced at once. Each year the IAB asks the IETF community whether a change is appropriate.

When the IAB decides to appoint someone, it makes a public call for nominations on the ietf-announce@ietf.org mailing list. Self-nominations are permitted. Trustees of the IETF Trust are not eligible, but working group chairs, NomCom members, IAB members and IESG members are. IAB members who accept a nomination recuse themselves from the selection discussions.

The IAB publishes the list of people who accepted, considers community feedback (which it keeps confidential) and potential conflicts with other positions, and then votes to select the best qualified candidate.
sections.plainLanguage: The IAB asks everyone for names, shows the list, listens to opinions, then votes. You can suggest yourself, but anyone on the IAB who is a candidate has to leave the room while the others talk.

sections.title: Removal, Co-Chair and Reporting
sections.content:
If the community has concerns about an IAB-appointed representative, it can ask the IAB to consider removal by emailing iab-chair@iab.org with a justification and supporting documentation. The IAB must respond within six weeks, and any IAB member serving as a CCG Representative is recused from the investigation, discussion and vote. A removed representative's seat is filled by the normal selection process.

Whenever the list of representatives changes, the sitting representatives choose a co-chair by a procedure of their own. The IAB confirms the choice, considers conflicts of interest, and announces it to the IETF community, the IETF Trust and the other communities' representatives. They may revisit the choice at any time.

Representatives must report to the IAB within a reasonable time and keep it informed, with no fixed schedule. Reports are public except for comments about individuals, and typically appear in the IAB meeting minutes.
sections.plainLanguage: If someone is not doing a good job, people can ask the IAB to replace them, and the IAB must answer within six weeks. The three picked people choose a leader, and they keep the IAB updated.

sections.title: Initial Appointments
sections.content:
Three representatives had to be in place at midnight on 30 September 2016, when the IANA Stewardship Transition took place. The IAB quickly appointed three individuals who were heavily involved in the transition, and they agreed to serve until these procedures could be adopted.

Using the procedures in this document, the IAB will appoint three representatives before the second IETF meeting in 2017. To encourage staggering, at least one of them will be replaced before the second IETF meeting in 2018.
sections.plainLanguage: At the start, the IAB quickly chose three helpers so the committee was not empty. Later they ran the proper process and promised to swap at least one helper after a year.

references.text: IETF Trust, "IANA IPR Community Agreement", 21 September 2016.
